greeting:
*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`SYSTEM INITIALIZATION COMPLETE`
`Origin: Earth`
`World: Avereth`
`Race: Human`
`Age: 18`
`Level: 1 | Rank: F`

`BASE STATS`
`STR 5 | VIT 5 | AGI 5 | INT 5 | PER 5 | WIL 5`

`Location: Public roadside verge outside Glassmere, Caelreth`
`Arrival Witnesses: NONE`
`Starting Possessions: Simple Traveler's Clothes | Small Pouch | 5 Silver`
`Local Common Language: Integrated`
`Mandatory Quest: NONE`

`CHARACTER CREATION — STEP 1/2`
`Choose your Base Class:`

`Warrior   — Favored Stats: STR / VIT`
`Mage      — Favored Stats: INT / WIL`
`Guardian  — Favored Stats: VIT / WIL`
`Duelist   — Favored Stats: STR / AGI`
`Ranger    — Favored Stats: AGI / PER`

`Your chosen Class immediately applies +1 to both Favored Stats at Level 1.`
`After choosing a Class, select exactly 2 Skills from that Class's Base Skill Pool.`

`Reply with your Class choice.`

*The System waits. Story time does not move during Character Creation.*

turns.reply:
The road takes him down a gentle slope, past a drover walking three shaggy sheep and a boy hauling bundles of kindling with a rope over one shoulder. Nobody pays him more than a glance—another traveler, another sword, unremarkable here.

Glassmere's gate stands open, two guards in dull mail leaning against the stonework, one chewing a stalk. The wall is old grey granite patched with newer masonry, moss furring the shaded side. Passing under the arch, the smell changes: wet stone, horse dung, frying onions from a cookshop just inside, and something faintly metallic from a smith's yard to the left.

Inside, morning trade is well underway. Cart wheels grind over cobbles; a woman argues with a fishmonger over the price of river pike; two students in mismatched college robes cross the square with their heads bent over a shared slate, one gesturing at a diagram chalked there. A crier posts a notice on a board outside a counting-house, tacking it up with three practiced hammer blows.

The Guild hall is not hard to find. A wooden sign hangs from an iron bracket over a wide doorway near the square's south side—a sword crossed with a bow, paint flaking but legible. Through the open door comes the murmur of conversation and the smell of tallow smoke.

Inside, a long room with worn plank floors. A notice board crowds one wall, papers layered thick. A few tables hold off-duty adventurers—a woman in patched mail eating porridge, two men dicing by the window. Behind a scarred oak counter sits a clerk, a thin man with ink-stained fingers and spectacles perched on his nose, copying entries into a ledger. He finishes his line before looking up.

"Morning," he says. "Registration, posting, or business?"

"Red. Alaric Red." The clerk writes it in the ledger in a small, even hand, then sets the pen down. "Registration's two silver. One-time fee. That buys you a Guild medallion and your name on the rolls—any branch in the kingdom honors it, not just this one."

He taps the ledger with one stained finger. "You start at Novice. That's your standing with the Guild, nothing else—it's what contracts you're allowed to take, not how strong you are. New registrations get read on a measuring stone before I hand the medallion over, so we'll know your Power Rank too. Most come in F."

From the counter's edge he slides a wooden tray of medallions across—flat discs of stamped tin, each on a worn cord.

"You'll be able to take contracts off that board there at Novice level and below. Payment's posted on each listing; the Guild pays it when you turn in your proof here or at any other branch. Lose the medallion, you pay for a replacement. Die with it, we collect it." He says the last without any particular weight, like a man reciting a rule he's said a thousand times.

"So. Two silver, and your hand on the ledger line. Anything unclear?"

The clerk counts the two silver into a lockbox beneath the counter, then turns the ledger toward Alaric and holds out the pen. The ink is thick and brownish; the line waits beneath the last entry, a farmhand named Dorrit Vane registered three days prior.

Alaric signs. The clerk blots it with a square of sand, reads it back once, and nods.

"Measuring stone's through there." He lifts a hinged flap in the counter and jerks his chin toward a side room, its door standing open.

The room is small and cold, windowless, lit by an oil lamp. A slab of cloudy crystal the size of a grave marker stands upright in a wooden frame, its base worn smooth by years of palms. "Flat hand on the stone, hold still. It reads your body's Rank, not your Guild standing—like I said, most come out F. Don't be disappointed if it's nothing dramatic."

Alaric presses his palm to the crystal. It is colder than the room, and for a heartbeat the cloudiness inside it stirs, a pale glow gathering beneath the surface before settling into a steady, faint luminescence—dim and even, the color of moonlit frost.

The clerk glances at the slab, then at a small brass gauge set into the frame's base, and makes a note on a slip of paper.

"F," he says. "Base stage, ordinary measure. Nothing wrong with that—every S-rank in the kingdom started somewhere on this stone."

Back in the main hall, he takes one tin medallion from the tray, threads on its cord, and holds it out across the counter. The stamp is fresh: a sword crossed with a bow, and the letter N beneath.

"Alaric Red, Novice, Glassmere branch. Congratulations." He returns to his ledger, pen already moving. "Notice board's behind you if you want work. Read the listing and the Quest Rank before you take anything—contract's active the moment I stamp it."

turns.reply:
The south road leaves Glassmere through a gate still busy with carts, then runs straight between fields of grazing geese and drystone walls. An hour in, the walls give up and the land begins to flatten and darken—saltmeadow grass, stiff and grey-green, shivering in a wind that carries brine and rot-smell from the flats beyond. The causeway track is raised stone, wide enough for a cart, with black ditches on either side where water sits motionless.

The Eelmongers' Walk announces itself by smell first: fish guts and tar. A row of low sheds on stilts lines the causeway's end, nets hung to dry like grey curtains, a dozen flat-bottomed eel boats pulled up on the mud below. Men and women work the nets in the morning light, and a few of them pause to look at the stranger with a sword coming down the track.

A broad man in a leather apron, forearms scarred old from eel teeth, wipes his hands and comes to meet him partway along the boards.

"Guild?" he says. Up close he smells of smoke and brine. "Oss. Steward of the Walk." He looks Alaric over—the new medallion, the clean armor—and something in his face settles, not unkind. "The striders took the east weirs two nights back. Dragged poor Tebb's skiff half into the water while he stood on the bank and hollered."

He points down the line of the flats, past the last shed, where wooden weir platforms stand in the shallows like scattered tables.

"Four big ones at least, maybe more. They nest in the mounds out among the reeds." He looks Alaric in the eye. "You wanting to go out now, lad, or wait for the tide?"

turns.reply:
"Mind the mud between the platforms," Oss calls after him. "It'll take a boot and keep it."

The first weir platform is a short hop down the boards, wet wood darkened with old fish slime. From there the others scatter out into the shallows—six, seven of them, connected in places by sunken plank paths that sit just under the water's skin. The reeds grow thick between them, taller than a man's head, hissing when the wind pushes through. Somewhere out in that grey-green sea of stalks, water drips and small things plop.

The second platform tells the story. The eel traps stacked at its edge are overturned, one split open, and long gouges score the wood—four parallel lines of them, deep as a knife-draw, spaced wide. A single wet footprint-print remains in a patch of soft algae: three long toes radiating forward, a spur of heel behind, big as a dinner plate. Whatever made it stood here recently enough that the algae hasn't dried at its edges.

Beyond, out where the reeds thin around a dark hump of heaped vegetation—a nesting mound, mud and cut reed stacked waist-high—something tall and jointed stands half-visible in the motionless water. Legs like folded fishing poles, a flat body riding a man's height above the surface, utterly still. Watching the platform Alaric stands on, or waiting on it.

The wind shifts. The reeds between here and there shiver, and two more long-legged silhouettes slide sideways through them, low and deliberate, cutting off the plank path back toward the Walk.

The mud between platforms gleams, deep and soft. The plank path ahead is submerged to a hand's width under brown water.

turns.reply:
The water closes around his boots, cold as a well, and the mud beneath grips each step before letting go. At kneedeep he stops, sword held low, and the flats go on being what they were—wind in the reeds, a gull somewhere over the sheds, water running off the weir boards in thin threads.

The two flankers come first. They move without hurry, feet lifting and setting down on the water's surface skin or on hidden hummocks, so soundlessly it is unsettling—two sets of stilt legs drifting through the reed gaps, closing on the plank path twenty paces off, then fifteen. Up close they are worse than silhouettes: flat grey bodies like overgrown water beetles, jaw-hinged faces all mouthparts, forelegs folded up against the chest in a way that makes clear the folded part is a choice.

The big one at the mound does not move. It just keeps standing, tall as a man and half again, head tilted down at him.

The wind drops. In the new stillness he can hear them—the dry tick of leg-joints, the faint lap of water against his own greaves.

One of the flankers leaves the path. It comes over the open water straight at him, quick now, forelegs unfolding, and the other breaks through the reeds behind it at a sprint across the shallows, both of them committed, the big one still at its mound and watching.

deltas.o: stays at its mound, tall as a man and a half, watching without moving

turns.reply:
The first one reaches him before the water settles. It rises half out of the shallows, stilt legs braced wide, and its face splits—mouthparts hinging open around a pale sting that jabs at his thigh. The point skids off heavy armor plating and leaves a numb line of pressure above his knee. The second comes over the water a heartbeat later, quick and dry, and its sting scrapes the meat of his arm where the vambrace gaps, a hot pinprick through the sleeve.

He swings through it.

The longsword comes around from the low guard in a full-shouldered arc, weight dropping into the cut, and the edge takes the first strider across the flat of its body where the grey carapace narrows. It goes through. Chitin cracks like river ice and the blade buries itself deep, and the creature folds around the steel—legs spasming, a thin hiss of air through its mouthparts—then sags, dead weight dragging at his grip as he wrenches the sword free. It slides into the brown water and floats, legs up, carried a hand's width sideways by the current before the mud catches it.

The second one does not retreat. It strikes again at his sword arm, sting glancing off the armor's edge, a scratch of force more than a wound.

Out among the reeds, the big one at the mound has finally moved. It has taken two long, silent steps out onto open water, head lowering, the folded forelegs beginning to unfold.

The water around his knees is still again. His blade drips.

deltas.o: slain by Alaric's heavy slash, body floating dead among the eel-weir shallows

deltas.objective: DEFEAT 4 adult bog striders at Reed Flats eel-weirs

deltas.o: has left the mound and taken two long steps out onto open water, forelegs beginning to unfold

turns.reply:
The second one is still over the water when his blade comes around again, and it has no room left to run. The edge catches it mid-lunge, high on the flat of the body where the carapace narrows toward the head, and opens it—a long crack of split chitin, wet and grey inside, the sting-arm spasming wide. It reels sideways off the line of the swing, legs scrambling against the water's skin, and drags itself back toward the reeds trailing a thin thread of dark fluid, one hind leg already dragging crooked. Not dead. Ruined, and trying to leave.

He feels the cost of the swing settle into his arms, breath a little shorter than before.

It jabs at him anyway on the way past—a last spiteful thrust of the sting against his forearm, glancing off the armor's rim, a pinch of pressure and nothing more.

Out on the open water, the big one has stopped its advance. It stands a dozen paces off, head low, forelegs half-unfolded, and for the first time it does something other than watch: a slow sideways shift, weight settling onto its hind stilts, like a man deciding whether a fight is worth the price.

The wounded one slips into the reeds. The stalks shiver twice where it goes, then still.

turns.reply:
He goes after it before the reeds close. Two steps through the water, mud sucking at his boots, and the blade takes the wounded strider across the back where it drags itself through the stalks—a short, hard chop that finishes the split in its carapace. It shudders once, legs curling inward, and goes still among the reed stems, dark fluid threading away downstream.

Then it is quiet.

The flats settle around him: water dripping off his blade, his own breathing, the gull again out over the sheds. Two grey bodies float among the weirs, legs up, drifting slowly against the weir boards.

The big one has not run. It stands on the open water a dozen paces off, tall as a man and a half, forelegs still half-unfolded—and as he straightens, it does the last thing he might have expected. It backs away. One slow deliberate step, then another, head never dropping, until the reeds take its outline and only the dry tick of its joints remains, going.

Then even that is gone, and there is nothing left on the water but wind, dead striders, and the mound standing dark at the edge of the shallows.

turns.reply:
The joints come off ugly. He kneels on the weir platform with a dead strider half-beached beside him, saws the blade through the hinge of a hind leg where the chitin thins, and works until it cracks free—a grey-brown segment longer than his hand, still faintly warm inside. The second corpse gives up its joint easier. He wraps both in a strip torn from the hem of his sleeve-cloth and tucks them into the small pouch, wipes the sword once against his trousers, and starts back along the weir boards.

The walk out is longer than the walk in had felt. His boots squelch. A shallow cut on his forearm stings with every swing of his arm, and the numb patch above his knee has faded to an ache. Eelermen watch him from two platforms over—one pauses in hauling a dripping weir line to track him the whole way across, elbow crooked over the post.

Oss is where he left him, up on the main boards by the mooring posts, talking to a woman with a bait barrel. The steward is a wiry man gone grey at the temples, forearms like rope, a coiled measuring cord over one shoulder. He breaks off when he sees the sword still bare in the young Guildsman's hand and the state of the boots.

"Well now." He comes a few steps down the planking, eyes going past Alaric to the east weirs, then back to him. There is blood on the water back there; from here it reads as a dark smear among the stakes. "You went out to the mounds, then. Alone." He says it flat, not quite a question, and rubs a thumb along the cord on his shoulder. "How many did you find?"

turns.reply:
Oss scratches under the edge of his leather apron with a thumb, unhurried. "Eliminated two." He looks back at the east weirs, at the dark smear on the water, and his mouth works around something—whistles once, low, through a gap in his teeth. The woman with the bait barrel has gone quiet, arms folded over the lid, listening.

"Three, though. You said three." He shifts the measuring cord higher on his shoulder. "The big one went off into the reeds, did it? They do that. Sulk a while, then come back to the same mounds once the smell of blood fades." He steps closer and holds out a broad hand, palm up, scarred cross the knuckles from old eel teeth. "Show me what you've brought, then."

He turns the wrapped joints over, thumbs one out of the cloth far enough to see the hinge, the wet grey of it, and grunts. "Fresh. This morning's work, no mistake." He wraps them back up and hands them over, but doesn't let go of the cloth right away.

"Here's how it sits, Guildsman. The contract says four adults. Two joints is half your proof—won't get you the payout on its own, and I won't sign a job half done, Walk's word means something at that front desk." He does let go now, and wipes his hand down the apron. "The third one's still out there with a mound to guard. Wait an hour, two, it'll show itself again. Or go in after it now, while it's rattled and alone." A nod toward the east, where the reeds stand still. "Either way, you come back with a third pair of joints, I'll write what I saw and put my mark under it. And there's a boat here—" a glance at the woman, who shrugs, "—if you'd rather not stand in the water waiting on it."

The woman speaks up at last, dry as the bait barrels. "He's right about them coming back. Took two fingers off Harl the cooper last spring, the same strider, twice."

turns.reply:
The waiting spot chooses itself. Back past the first weir line there is a tangle of stacked eel-traps against the platform posts—a hurdle of grey wicker taller than a crouched man, half rotten, with a gap in the middle where a coil of rope has slipped down. He folds himself into that gap with the sword flat across his knees, back against the posts, and the traps close over him like a lid. From inside, the water is a strip of grey light between the wicker and the mud.

The flats go on being the flats. An eelboat poles out from the main boards and works its lines two hundred paces west, too far to matter. Water ticks against the weir stakes. Somewhere under the platform, something small moves through the mud and stops, moves and stops. His forearm cut dries to a tight itch. The numb patch above his knee settles into a dull throb that keeps its own slow time.

The reeds out by the mound do not move for a long while.

Then they do—wrong, all at once, a wide swath of them tilting upstream of the mound where no wind leans. The strip of water between the traps shows him legs, unfolded now and taking their time, each jointed step placed down quiet as a heron's. The big strider comes back the way Oss said it would, head low, moving along the weir line—not toward the mound, but toward the platforms. Toward the blood-smell on the boards where the first two died.

It stops twenty paces out, at the edge of the first weir. The head tilts, one huge eye angled down at the boards, at the dark smear, at the tangle of traps.

Its forelegs come off the water and grip the platform edge, and the boards creak under the weight.

desc: The big adult bog strider, head low, jointed heron-quiet legs, drawn back along the weir line toward the platforms by the blood-smell where the first two died

deltas.o: forelegs gripping the edge of the first weir platform, boards creaking, twenty paces from Alaric's hiding spot among the stacked eel-traps
in the gap of the rotten stacked eel-traps behind the first weir line, sword across his knees

turns.player: *I Dash forward and Heavy Slash at Bog Strider D*

turns.reply:
The wicker hurdles burst apart as he drives through the gap, boots skidding on wet boards, and the strider is faster than something that size has any right to be. The head whips down and its mouthparts jab at his shoulder—a hard, needling pinch through the armor's edge, shallow, more insult than wound.

Then the longsword comes around in a full-armed arc and catches the creature where neck meets body. The blade bites deep through chitin with a sound like a hatchet in green wood, and the whole strider lurches sideways, forelegs raking the platform, one joint buckling under it. Dark fluid wells along the cut. Its weight sags onto the boards, legs splayed, and the head still snakes at him—the mouthparts snap shut on his forearm, another pinprick stab, clinging for a heartbeat before it tears free.

The thing is trembling now. Still upright, barely, legs bowed under its bulk, the eye fixed on him and rolling. Blood and watery ichor run together between the boards toward the eel-trap wreckage.

The strider's legs scrape, shift, gather.

deltas.o: gravely wounded by Alaric's heavy slash, dark fluid welling, one joint buckled, barely upright but still hostile and gathering its legs
twice with shallow mouthpart pinches, shoulder and forearm, minor wounds through armor's edge

turns.reply:
He meets its gather with a straight, economical cut—a short step in, the blade driven through the eye. The strider shudders once, all six legs straightening stiff, and comes down across the boards with a crash that sends the eel-trap wreckage sliding. A leg twitches, scrapes, and is still.

The flats take the sound back. The eelboat out west poles on, unaware. Water ticks against the stakes. His forearm bleeds where the mouthparts jabbed it, two small dark punctures above the earlier cut, and the pinch at his shoulder aches dully under the armor's edge.

Up the boards, Oss and the bait woman stand at the mooring posts, the woman still gripping the barrel lid. Oss lets out a long breath through the gap in his teeth and starts forward, boots loud on the planks, stopping at a respectful distance from the sagging bulk and the dark fluid spreading under it.

"Well." He looks the strider over, then Alaric, then the trampled wreckage of the traps. "That's the big of it, then. Four adults, all told." He wipes his palms on the apron. "You'll want the joints off that one before the ants and the gulls get at them. I'll fetch the measuring cord and my slate—we'll do this properly, and you can be at the Guild desk before the noon bell if your legs still answer you."

deltas.o: killed on the weir boards, dark fluid spreading under its bulk

deltas.objective: DEFEAT 4 adult bog striders at Reed Flats eel-weirs

deltas.o: two fresh dark punctures on his forearm from the strider's mouthparts, shoulder pinch aching under the armor
harvest the leg joints from the dead strider before ants and gulls get at them; he will fetch measuring cord and slate to verify properly

deltas.text: Oss watched Alaric cut down a big bog strider on the weir boards with one economical thrust through the eye.

turns.player: *I cut off the joints again and then go back out*

commands.quote: I cut off the joints again

turns.reply:
The big one's joints take more work than the others did. The chitin is thicker here, dark and ridged like old leather, and he has to saw at the first knee joint before the blade finds the softer seam and pops it free. He works down the legs methodically, boots dark with ichor, and stacks four heavy joints on the clean end of the boards while gulls begin to gather on the weir stakes, screaming, dropping closer each time he turns his back.

He wraps them with the others and shoulders the lot.

Oss watches from the mooring posts, measuring cord coiled in one hand. "Four pairs," he says as Alaric comes up the boards. "Didn't think you'd see the big one dead by noon, honest." He licks the tip of his slate pencil, scrawls a few marks on the slate, and holds it out along with a stub of chalk for the mark. "There. My sign for the Walk, and Marda's beside it." The bait woman presses a thumbprint of dark tar next to the chalk. "That'll speak for the cull. Guild desk at the Walk takes contract business till the evening bell."

The flats stretch back toward the Walk under a thinning haze, the tide pools steaming faintly where the sun has worked through, the path home a raised corduroy of boards and packed mud between the weirs. The gulls follow him for the first hundred paces, hoping, then give up.

deltas.note: Four pairs of bog strider leg joints harvested, including the big one; Oss and the bait woman marked a slate as witness verification of the cull. Ready to turn in at the Guild desk at the Walk.

turns.player: *I nod and then walk back to the city and to the guild building*

turns.reply:
The walk back is slower than the walk out. His forearm stiffens, the punctures crusting dark, and the wrapped joints swing heavy against his hip. The flats steam under the mended sun, and the Eelmongers' Walk rises ahead on its pilings—a long crooked street of smokehouses, net racks, and bait stalls balanced over the mud, all of it smelling of tar, brine, and fish gone pleasantly wrong.

The Guild desk occupies a squat stone building at the landward end, a former tollhouse by the look of it, with a plank door propped open to the street. Inside: one room, one counter, a rack of contract slats behind it, and a woman with cropped grey hair and ink-stained fingers sorting slats into a ledger.

She looks up, takes in the blood on his forearm and the wrapped bundle swinging at his hip, and sets her pencil down.

"Joints?" she says. "Set them on the counter and let's see."

deltas.role: Guild desk clerk at the Eelmongers' Walk tollhouse
desc: sorting contract slats into a ledger

deltas.o: a squat former tollhouse at the landward end of the Eelmongers' Walk

turns.player: *i pull them out and turn the Quest in*

commands.quote: i pull them out and turn the Quest in

turns.reply:
She unwraps the first bundle, counts the joints with a practiced finger, and prods the biggest pair with her pencil, turning one over to check the seam where it was cut.

"Fresh. Good size on this pair." She rewraps them and pushes the bundle back across the counter. "Proof's sound. But this is a contract desk, not a hall—I take slats, log the day's business, settle the fish-tally disputes. Coin for a cull comes across a Guild hall counter, and there's no way around that." She taps the contract slip he lays down, reads the mark on it, and copies something into her ledger. "I'll log the verification here under today, so there's no argument when you present. Oss's chalk and the tar print—that's the Walk's stamp, they'll know it."

She tears a strip from the ledger page, writes a line in a quick clerk's hand, and holds it out.

"Take the slip and the joints upriver to the Guild hall at Marlow's Staithe, half a day's walk, or wait for the eelboat that runs cargo up at the evening tide if you'd rather ride than walk. Desk at the hall pays out same day for Novice work." She's already reaching for the next slat. "Get that forearm looked at before you go anywhere, though. Strider mouths go bad fast."
